clue.text: Handy handbooks, certainly portable

parts.note: the Latin phrase behind these guidebooks means 'go with me', so they are by name books to carry about

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin name means 'go with me', which is why 'certainly portable' fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Such books are small reference guides kept constantly at hand, carried in a pocket.

clue.text: Life of model for Orlando

definitions.meaning: the Latin word for life, also used for a biography or a CV
Virginia Woolf based the hero of her novel Orlando on her lover

explanation.definitionFit: Latin for life, and the first name of Sackville-West, whom Woolf's Orlando portrays.

clue.text: Smiles performed it

parts.note: Samuel Smiles, the Victorian author of Self-Help, wrote a book of this title; the surface reads as someone grinning while doing an obligation

explanation.surface: A cheerful person carries out a task.
explanation.walkthrough: Smiles is Samuel Smiles, the Victorian moralist, whose 1880 book bears the answer's title; 'performed' points to the other sense of doing what is required.
explanation.definitionFit: An obligation is something one performs, and the moralist Samuel Smiles wrote a book with that one-word title.

clue.text: Arriviste Dickens wife putting a good face on things

definitions.text: Arriviste Dickens wife putting a good face on things

parts.words: Arriviste Dickens wife putting a good face on things
parts.note: the social-climbing couple in Our Mutual Friend have a surname meaning a thin attractive surface layer, and here it is the wife

explanation.surface: A newly rich Victorian wife keeps up appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Our Mutual Friend the Veneerings are brand-new social climbers; a veneer is a thin attractive layer over cheap material, hence 'putting a good face on things'.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the parvenu hostess of Our Mutual Friend, whose surname names a showy surface coating.

clue.text: Shavian prodigy who preferred solitary contemplation of mathematics

definitions.text: Shavian prodigy who preferred solitary contemplation of mathematics

parts.words: Shavian prodigy who preferred solitary contemplation of mathematics
parts.note: in the last part of Shaw's Back to Methuselah a young woman of the far future tires of her lover and turns to mathematics

explanation.surface: A gifted young character in a Shaw play would rather do sums alone.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the young woman in Shaw's Back to Methuselah who abandons Strephon for abstract thought.

clue.text: Robert Owen wrote of inmates' changed characters

indicators.note: the letters of the words before are altered and set in a new order

explanation.surface: The social reformer Robert Owen wrote about how prisoners' natures were reformed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed characters' rearranges the letters of OF INMATES. Robert Owen, the Welsh social reformer, published a manifesto in 1840; the clue's letter count is missing as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: The reformer Robert Owen issued a public declaration of his principles, a document of exactly this kind.

clue.text: It's easily located in fifteenth-century literature

definitions.text: It's easily located in fifteenth-century literature

parts.words: It's easily located in fifteenth-century literature
parts.note: an archaic adjective meaning simple is found all over medieval writing

explanation.surface: Something is simple to find in medieval writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the old word meaning 'easy' or 'easily', so 'easily located' is a pun: the word for easily is what you find there.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic Middle English adjective and adverb meaning easy, found in medieval literature.

clue.text: Old historian — I deduct his odd spelling in modern texts, prefer Nicholls's 1550 version

indicators.note: letters spelt out in an odd way signals the words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A note on how an ancient Greek historian's name was spelt in Tudor translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd spelling' rearranges I DEDUCT HIS. The rest of the clue is commentary: modern texts spell the Greek historian with a Y, but Thomas Nicolls's 1550 English translation used this I spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian who wrote of the Peloponnesian War, here in Nicolls's Tudor spelling.

clue.text: Eponymous girl in verse from tall chap, and from curtailed poet

definitions.text: Eponymous girl in verse from tall chap, and from curtailed poet

parts.words: Eponymous girl in verse from tall chap, and from curtailed poet
parts.note: a heroine who gives her name to a narrative poem by Longfellow, whose name read playfully means a tall chap

explanation.surface: A girl named in a poem comes from a lanky man and a poet cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tall chap' is a pun on Longfellow (long fellow), whose 1847 poem is named after its Acadian heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: The title heroine of Longfellow's poem about the Acadian exile, so the girl gives the poem its name.

clue.text: Peake character in terminal state

parts.note: the final Gormenghast novel by Mervyn Peake leaves its hero without companions, the title naming him in that last state

explanation.surface: A fictional figure is near death.
explanation.walkthrough: Mervyn Peake's Gormenghast books end with a third volume naming its hero and his solitary condition; 'terminal' means both final in the series and dying.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the last Gormenghast novel, which shows the hero by himself.

clue.text: Moon opposite to Borges

parts.note: the Spanish word for the moon begins the title of Borges's 1925 collection, Moon Across the Way

explanation.surface: A moon faces the Argentine writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Borges's early poetry book is Luna de enfrente, 'Moon Across the Way', so 'opposite' translates 'de enfrente'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish and Latin for the moon, as in the title of Borges's poetry collection.

clue.text: She disparaged the Brodie set"

parts.note: in Muriel Spark's novel Miss Mackay, who runs the school, despises Jean Brodie's favourite girls

explanation.surface: A woman sneered at a group of girls.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, Miss Mackay, in charge of the Marcia Blaine School, is hostile to the 'Brodie set'.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Mackay is the principal of the girls' school in Spark's novel and Brodie's adversary.

clue.text: Bondsman's brother said to be safe with Belgian

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
a Fleming is a Flemish-speaking native of Belgium

explanation.surface: A man is reported to be secure in the company of a Belgian.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Bondsman' is Ian Fleming, creator of James Bond; his elder brother was the travel writer. 'Peter' is safebreakers' slang for a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: The travel writer was the elder brother of Ian, the novelist who created James Bond.

clue.text: Sort of loon serving Macbeth

parts.note: Macbeth curses a pale frightened servant with a famous insult describing his complexion

explanation.surface: A kind of diving bird waits on a Scottish king.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth Act 5 the king abuses a terrified servant: 'The devil damn thee black, thou cream-faced loon!' A loon is also a bird, the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's insult for his pale, frightened servant describes a face white with fear.

clue.text: Moment for a dramatic flop from Ben Travers? …

definitions.text: Moment for a dramatic flop from Ben Travers?

parts.words: Moment for a dramatic flop from Ben Travers?
parts.note: a flop on stage is slang for a failed show, and Ben Travers wrote an Aldwych farce whose title also means the Christmas season

explanation.surface: Asking when a playwright's show failed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Travers wrote Aldwych farces, one titled for the Christmas season; a 'turkey' is slang for a theatrical failure, hence 'dramatic flop'.
explanation.definitionFit: The festive season is named after its bird, and a failed play is called by that bird's name too; it is a Travers farce.

clue.text: What may be called 'the board' of some of these 'is numbered to thirty two" (Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor)

definitions.text: What may be called 'the board' of some of these 'is numbered to thirty two" (Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor)

parts.words: What may be called 'the board' of some of these 'is numbered to thirty two" (Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor)
parts.note: Mayhew describes street gambling tables with numbered pockets where a ball settles after spinning

explanation.surface: A quotation from Mayhew on street gambling apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Mayhew's survey of Victorian street life describes portable gambling wheels whose boards were numbered.
explanation.definitionFit: These are gambling wheels with numbered slots, as Mayhew's street gamblers carried.

clue.text: … transmitted to veiled set, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words before may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Something was broadcast to a set that was covered up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges VEILED SET. The clue follows on from 14-down with dots.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that was broadcast has been put out on the small screen.

clue.text: Bore introduces dull reading in Latin literature

indicators.note: the openings of the following words introduce them, so their first letters are taken

explanation.surface: A dull book is brought into the study of Latin texts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduces' takes the first letter of each of DULL READING IN LATIN LITERATURE. 'Bore' wants to be a tedious person; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bore a hole is to make one with a rotating tool, the same as to make a hole with one.

clue.text: Experimental writer sees first koala in maple

indicators.note: in places the next piece inside the maple

parts.note: Acer is the botanical name of the maple genus

indicators.note: first means only the first letter of koala is used

explanation.surface: An avant-garde author spots a koala up a maple tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Kathy Acker was an American experimental novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Kathy Acker was an American avant-garde novelist known for collage and plagiarism techniques.

clue.text: Power of Hardy is lukewarm

definitions.meaning: Paula Power is the heroine of Thomas Hardy's novel A ..., the title describing her
lukewarm means half-hearted, indifferent in religion or politics

explanation.definitionFit: The word describes someone half-hearted, like the church at Laodicea in Revelation, and titles Hardy's novel about Paula Power.

clue.text: Short calls, such as that of Hitler related by

annotationWithheld.clue: Short calls, such as that of Hitler related by

clue.text: George Moore's greeting may be soothing

definitions.meaning: the second volume of George Moore's trilogy Hail and Farewell (Ave, ..., Vale) is the Latin greeting
an ointment that eases or soothes

explanation.definitionFit: It is Latin for 'be well', the middle volume of Moore's memoirs, and a soothing balm.

clue.text: Corneille protagonist likely to give wrong impression

definitions.meaning: Corneille's comedy Le Menteur has the deceiving Dorante as its title character
one who tells untruths and so misleads

explanation.definitionFit: Corneille's Le Menteur names its title character a teller of untruths, someone who deceives.

clue.text: Haiku poet from Paris, Saint Cloud

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Japanese poet comes from the Parisian suburb of Saint-Cloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to letters inside 'Paris, Saint'. Kobayashi Issa was a great Japanese haiku master. 'Cloud' only completes the place name Saint-Cloud for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Kobayashi Issa is one of the four great masters of Japanese haiku.

clue.text: Fratricidal crime writer?

parts.note: the first murderer in Genesis killed his brother Abel

explanation.surface: Asking about a writer of murder stories who killed a sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: James M. Cain wrote The Postman Always Rings Twice; his surname is also that of Abel's brother in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical murderer of his brother shares his name with the American crime novelist James M. Cain.

clue.text: Priest's ale spilt, rite lapses disastrously in ruins of sterile spa as reptiles seen wandering toward stringed instruments

indicators.note: ale that is spilt runs everywhere, signalling the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: the possessive is read with its s as a letter, giving the full word priests

explanation.surface: A comic chain of spilt drink, lapsed rites, ruined spas and wandering reptiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spilt' rearranges PRIESTS ALE. The clue is a joke: 'rite lapses', 'sterile spa' and 'as reptiles' are each further anagrams of the answer, signalled by 'disastrously', 'ruins' and 'wandering'.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalteries are ancient plucked zithers, instruments with strings.

clue.text: Book said to be commonplace, though could be one of!

definitions.text: Book said to be commonplace, though could be one of!

parts.words: Book said to be commonplace, though could be one of!
parts.note: a commonplace book of notes, with a pun on the Latin plural that sounds like an opponent, of whom it could be one

explanation.surface: A book is called ordinary, though it might be one of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word means a collection of miscellaneous notes, a commonplace book; it also resembles 'adversary', so it 'could be one of' them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin term denotes a notebook of miscellaneous jottings, the scholar's commonplace book.
